earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
notes: From the Barks rendering beginning 'Today, like every other day, we wake up empty and frightened... Take down a musical instrument. Let the beauty we love be what we do. There are hundreds of ways to kneel and kiss the ground.' The corpus text alters 'we love' to 'you love', a common web variant. Barks worked from earlier English translations rather than the Persian, so the English wording is his; the underlying poem is genuinely Rumi's. Cannot place the Persian original (Divan-e Shams ghazal) from memory.

earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
notes: A Barks rendering of a Rumi quatrain; I recall it in The Essential Rumi with consistent attribution across reputable Rumi collections. Wording is Barks' English, not a literal translation. No Persian source located from memory.

I cannot place this line in any Rumi translation I know — not Barks, Nicholson, Arberry, or Helminski. The theological compression ('you must become God') is unlike the standard renderings, which speak of annihilation in the Beloved rather than becoming God. Possibly a loose paraphrase of a fana passage, possibly a modern invention. Honest answer: unknown.

Cannot place this in any Rumi translation. The grain-of-sand-becomes-pearl motif is a stock modern inspirational image; the flat declarative diction here matches none of the standard English Rumi translators. Circulates on quote sites without any cited source. Likely a modern composition attached to Rumi's name, but I have no evidence of a true author.

Rumi does use the rider-who-cannot-see-his-own-mount figure (the Mathnawi has teaching stories about a man searching for the animal he is riding), so the image is authentically Rumi's. But I cannot place this exact English sentence in any translation, and it reads like a paraphrase rather than a rendering. Image plausible, wording unverified.

earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
notes: A well-known Barks rendering of a Rumi quatrain, appearing in The Essential Rumi. Attribution to Rumi is consistent across reputable collections; the English phrasing ('Lovers don't finally meet somewhere. They're in each other all along.') is Barks'. Persian original not identified from memory.

I recall this short line from Coleman Barks' Rumi versions and believe it appears in The Essential Rumi, but I am not confident enough in the specific volume to cite it as a print source. Attribution to Rumi (via Barks) is consistent in the sources I know; the underlying Persian is not identified.

One of the most heavily circulated 'Rumi' lines on the internet and one of the most doubted. I cannot place it in Barks, Nicholson, Arberry, Helminski, or any other translation, and its vocabulary ('your task', 'barriers within yourself') is modern therapeutic English rather than Sufi poetics — it reads closer to twentieth-century self-help or A Course in Miracles-adjacent writing than to a thirteenth-century ghazal. I suspect it is not Rumi, but I cannot name a true author, so I am not asserting a reattribution.

I have a weak recollection of this line in a Barks-style Rumi rendering (sometimes quoted with a following sentence about the body's purity), but I cannot confirm the volume or the Persian original. The imagery is consistent with Rumi's treatment of the body as woven of light. Attribution plausible, evidence thin.

Among the most quoted Rumi lines in English, and consistently attributed to him via Coleman Barks' versions. However, Rumi scholars (Omid Safi among them) have noted that Barks' most famous lines often have no close Persian counterpart, and I cannot point to the ghazal or Mathnawi passage behind this one. Attribution is consistent but the sourcing chain stops at a modern English rendering, so I am not putting it above the promotion bar.

Cannot place this line. Alchemical gold imagery is genuinely Rumi's territory (the Beloved as the philosopher's stone that transmutes copper to gold), but this specific one-sentence formulation appears only on quote aggregators with no source. Unknown.

earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
notes: A recognized Coleman Barks rendering ('Dance, when you're broken open...'), appearing in The Essential Rumi and widely reprinted with consistent attribution to Rumi. English wording is Barks'; Persian original not identified from memory.

earliest_print_source: "No Frames, No Boundaries," Russell Schweickart, address to the Lindisfarne Association, July 1974
notes: This is the well-documented passage from Apollo 9 astronaut Rusty Schweickart's 1974 Lindisfarne talk 'No Frames, No Boundaries,' delivered in the second person as he recounts his EVA and the view of Earth. It has been reprinted many times, including in Lindisfarne conference collections and in Kevin Kelley's photo-and-text anthology The Home Planet (1988). I am confident of the speaker and the talk; I am less certain of which reprint carries this exact excerpt, so I have cited the original address rather than a page. Note the corpus author field carries the redundant title suffix 'Astronaut'.

Sabrina Ward Harrison is a real author-artist (Spilling Open: The Art of Becoming Yourself, 1999; Brave on the Rocks, 2000), and this aphorism's register fits her handwritten-journal books. But I cannot place the line in a specific title, and the thought is a commonplace of Buddhist-inflected popular writing, so it could easily have drifted onto her name. Unconfirmed.

This does not read as Augustine in any register — not the Confessions, not the City of God, not the sermons — and 'a life worth remembering' as a route to 'immortality' inverts Augustine's actual theology, where immortality is God's gift and earthly fame is explicitly disparaged. The line circulates far more commonly attributed to Bruce Lee, in the sayings collected from his notebooks and popularized posthumously; that attribution is itself unverified, so I am flagging the Augustine attribution as wrong without asserting Lee as confirmed.
suggested_reattribution: Widely circulated as Bruce Lee (that attribution is itself unverified); not Augustine

notes: Consistently attributed to Salvador Dali across quotation dictionaries and Dali literature, and the sentiment matches his public persona of grandiose self-deprecation. I cannot name the interview, book, or date of first appearance, so the sourcing chain is secondary only. Attribution steady, primary source not established.

Johnson wrote at length on fear in The Rambler (No. 126 contains the well-known 'Fear is implanted in us as a preservative from evil; but its duty, like that of other passions, is not to overbear reason, but to assist it'), and this sentence is stylistically compatible with that essay. But the crisp epigrammatic form suggests a later condensation of Johnson's prose rather than his own sentence, and I cannot confirm the exact wording in any Rambler or Idler number. Plausible but unconfirmed; deliberately not citing a number I cannot verify.

Genuine Johnson, from The Idler essay on the disappointment of anticipated pleasures. The original punctuates it as two sentences ('Pleasure is very seldom found where it is sought. Our brightest blazes of gladness are commonly kindled by unexpected sparks.'); the corpus joins them with a semicolon. I am confident of the essay and confident of Johnson; the 1759 date follows the Idler's run in the Universal Chronicle.

earliest_print_source: Recollections of the Table-Talk of Samuel Rogers, Alexander Dyce, 1856
notes: A stock Regency epigram consistently credited to the poet and celebrated conversationalist Samuel Rogers (1763-1855), whose remarks survive chiefly through Dyce's posthumous Table-Talk. Quotation dictionaries routinely source Rogers quips to that volume and I believe this is one of them, but I cannot confirm the page or that this specific quip appears there rather than in another memoir of Rogers, so treat the citation as probable rather than checked.

Attributed only to an anonymous collective ('Samurai maxim'), which is not an attribution at all. I cannot trace it to Hagakure, the Book of Five Rings, Budoshoshinshu, or any classical bushido text, and the English is modern. Most 'samurai maxims' in circulation are twentieth-century Western compositions. Origin unknown.

Sanaya Roman and Duane Packer are real co-authors whose Creating Money: Keys to Abundance (1988) covers exactly this material, so the pairing of quote to authors is plausible. I cannot confirm this sentence appears in that book or in another of their titles. Also note the author field misspells the second name as 'Duane Pack' (should be Duane Packer) and so does not match q_1248's spelling.

Consistent in content and voice with the Roman/Packer Earth Life Series (Creating Money, Living with Joy, Spiritual Growth), but I cannot place the sentence in a specific volume or year. Real authors, plausible attribution, no confirmable source.

Sandra Anne Taylor is a real author (Quantum Success, Secrets of Attraction, Truth, Triumph and Transformation) and the vocabulary of 'self-honoring choices' and 'authentic power' fits that genre and era. I cannot locate this passage in any specific title of hers. Unconfirmed. The corpus text also retains stray enclosing quotation marks and an anomalous capital after a semicolon.

Widely circulated with consistent attribution to Sara Paddison, and usually to her book The Hidden Power of the Heart (Planetary Publications / HeartMath, 1992), which is a real title on exactly this subject. I have not confirmed the page or verified the excerpt against the text, so I am recording the attribution as consistent secondary evidence rather than citing the book as a checked source. The trailing ellipsis indicates the passage is truncated.

Same author and same idiom as q_1250 — the heart-intelligence language ('surrender your head to your heart', 'the real teacher is within you') is characteristic HeartMath-school writing and consistent with Sara Paddison's The Hidden Power of the Heart (1992). But this longer passage is less commonly quoted than q_1250 and I cannot place it in a specific chapter or confirm it is not stitched together from separate paragraphs. Plausible, unconfirmed.
